synopsis: EMESRT PR-5A Revision 3.0, dated September 2024, supplies the nine-layer vehicle-interaction model: controls run from site requirements through operator awareness at Level 7, advisory controls at Level 8, and automatic slowing and stopping at Level 9 [f2120, f4080, f6229]. Level 9 is a machine-control capability rather than a standalone product, and effective upper-level controls require understanding and maintaining the Level 1–7 baseline; site conditions can make the same braking algorithm safe in one location and troublesome in another [f2585, f11750, f11753]. Regulatory emphasis differs: NSW and NIOSH favor lower-level controls with collision systems as backup, while South Africa mandated Level 9 for surface and underground trackless mobile mining machinery from 21 December 2022 without a transitional period; one earlier trade report instead suggested December 2023 [f3624, f1087, f1088, f1364]. That mandate pushed deployment followed by refinement, whereas Epiroc recommends evaluation before enforcing Level 9, and EMESRT/ICMM warn that unqualified deployment can impair production and accelerate brake wear [f359, f6420, f2892]. Wabtec's December 2021 Komatsu haul-truck tests demonstrated controlled deceleration up to 30 km/h but still relied on physical testing to adjust detection zones, while the reviewed sources yielded no public simulation-validated Level 9 collision-avoidance evidence from mining OEMs [f1345, f1247, f4128]. The ACARP framework separates proving object detection from proving Level 8 or 9 intervention, reinforcing the need to validate both sensing and machine response rather than treating the Level 9 label as sufficient evidence [f559, f11752].
